answer: The plan is strong on problem validation and early traction, but several gaps and inconsistencies would weaken it with a skeptical judge. Priority fixes: (1) Fix the financial math. The market sizing mixes figures: 4 adapters x $89 = $356 hardware and $468/yr subscription per shop, but 60,000 shops would yield ~$21M hardware and ~$28M software, not $28M each. Year-one revenue of $61,000 on 640 adapters (~$57K hardware alone) plus 160 shops of subscriptions (~$75K annualized, less if ramping) does not reconcile with the stated $824/shop figure. 'Each 1% = 600 shops' is right, but tie it to a bottom-up ramp. Add a simple quarterly model with assumptions on churn, ramp timing and unit economics so numbers can be audited. (2) Reconcile traction claims. 41 pre-orders at $3,649 implies ~1 adapter per shop, far below the assumed 4 per shop, and 17 committed subscribers is not yet paid revenue. State clearly what is paid vs. verbally committed, and explain how average adapters per shop will rise. (3) Strengthen the evidence behind claims. The 2.5% accuracy result should include test conditions (wrench types, angles, temperature, operator variation, drift over time, battery life) and whether it meets ISO 6789 or a relevant standard. A 38-interview sample from presumably local shops should be framed as directional, and the plan should show willingness to pay evidence beyond the pre-orders (price sensitivity, who signs the check). (4) Address the central risks head-on. Add a risk section covering: technician adoption and behavior (will techs actually clip on and scan every job?), tampering or falsified logs, liability if the device reads wrong or gives false assurance (the product could create the very exposure it aims to reduce), calibration drift and recalibration cost, and whether insurers or customers will actually value the report. (5) Sharpen the competitive and defensibility case. Competitors are dismissed too quickly: name specific products and prices (e.g., digital torque adapters, Snap-on/Gearwrench/CDI smart tools, shop-management software that could add checklists) and explain why a tool maker or software incumbent cannot copy this. The 'calibration algorithm' and 'spec library' need a plan for protection (patent filing, data moat) and honest acknowledgment that torque specs are public. (6) Make the go-to-market concrete. $140 CAC through trade shows and distributors is asserted without evidence; show channel-level assumptions, the sales cycle, and the distributor partnership status. Explain how a $39/month subscription is justified relative to shop-management software already in use and whether integration with those systems is planned. (7) Close team and execution gaps. The team is all students with one hardware engineer; identify who owns manufacturing, certification (FCC/CE for Bluetooth) and quality control, and whether students will commit full-time after graduation. Name the advisor and any manufacturing mentor. Clarify the unformed legal entity, IP ownership (university grant and student-inventor IP assignment issues), and cap table before accepting prize money. (8) Tighten the ask. Show a milestone-based use of funds, why $24K covers 500 units plus certification (unit BOM cost, tooling, tolerances for defects), and what the next raise looks like after this prize. The plan projects break-even in Q4 of year two on $40K plus $22K raised; show cash runway and burn to support that. (9) Presentation: lead the summary with a one-line value proposition and the top two traction metrics, add a labeled assumptions table, cite sources for the 180,000-shop and 5-technician figures, and cut repetition so the document is easier to scan.
